title: The Gut and the Hype
paragraphs: For most of the twentieth century, the bacteria living in the human gut were regarded chiefly as passengers, tolerated rather than studied. That view has shifted dramatically since the United States National Institutes of Health launched the Human Microbiome Project in 2007, an effort to catalogue the microbes that inhabit healthy people. Researchers now know that these communities help break down dietary fibre that our own enzymes cannot digest, producing short-chain fatty acids that the body can use as a source of energy.

Popular accounts often add that microbial cells outnumber human ones by ten to one, a figure repeated for decades. Yet a 2016 analysis by Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs and Ron Milo concluded that the ratio is closer to one to one, with roughly as many bacteria as human cells in a reference adult man. The correction did not diminish the importance of gut microbes, but it illustrated how readily a striking number can harden into accepted fact.

A similar caution applies to the flood of studies linking particular microbial profiles to obesity, depression or autoimmune disease. Many of these findings are associations observed at a single moment, and it is easy to conflate such a pattern with a cause. An illness might alter the microbiome rather than the reverse, or diet and medication might shape both at once. Disentangling these possibilities usually requires controlled experiments, which are slow and expensive to run in people.

There are, nonetheless, cases in which manipulating the microbiome has proved its worth. In 2022 the US Food and Drug Administration approved the first faecal microbiota product, intended to prevent recurrence of Clostridioides difficile infection in adults after antibiotic treatment. The lesson is not that microbial science has been oversold in every respect, but that its strongest claims are those tested against a specific outcome.
